message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm the asshole in this situation. Let me break it down step by step. First, my co-worker asked me to cover his shift so he could attend his sister's memorial. The shift is from 2pm to 10pm, or maybe 3pm to 10pm. He knew about his schedule a week in advance because our workplace schedules us every Tuesday. So, he's been aware of his shift for at least a week before he asked me. Our workplace has an employee attendance system where you can request someone to cover part of your shift. If no one is available, you can text people directly. My co-worker tried that system, but no one was available, so he messaged me. I hate my job, so when he asked, I said I couldn't come in, even though I was free. He's asked me before, and I covered his shift once. I also asked him to cover one of my shifts later, so we're even. After I declined, he replied with "Of course not," which made me feel bad. Hmm, so is it wrong for me to decline? I mean, I hate the job, but it's about a memorial service. That's a significant event. He knew about his shift a week in advance, so maybe he should have planned earlier or found someone else. But he did try the system first, and when that didn't work, he asked me. I covered his shift once before, so maybe I should have done it again, especially for something important like a memorial. But I also don't want to feel like I'm always the one covering shifts. We were even, so maybe it's fair that I declined this time. On the other hand, his response made me feel like an asshole, which is harsh. Maybe he was upset and took it out on me, but I still wonder if I should have helped him out, especially since it's a family matter. I think the main points are: the request was for a memorial, he tried the system first, I had declined before but also asked him to cover mine, and my job is something I hate. So, is it wrong to say no, or is it understandable given my feelings about the job? I'm leaning towards maybe I should have helped, but I also don't want to be taken advantage of. It's a tough spot.
